title: Fenwick Tree: Range Add, Point Query
oneLiner: Design a RangeAdder with addRange(left, right, delta) and get(index), both O(log n), by keeping a difference array inside a Fenwick tree.
keyTakeaway: Turn a range update into two point updates with a difference array: add delta at left and -delta at right + 1, and the current value at i is the original nums[i] plus the prefix sum of the differences up to i. A Fenwick tree does both of those in O(log n): add climbs with i += i & -i, prefix descends with i -= i & -i.
explanation:
Build a class RangeAdder over an int array with addRange(left, right, delta), which adds delta to every element from left to right inclusive, and get(index), which returns the current value of nums[index]. Looping over the range makes addRange O(n); the goal is O(log n) for both.

Step 1, the difference array. Keep diff where diff[i] is how much element i has changed relative to element i - 1 since the start. Adding delta to [left, right] only changes two differences: diff[left] += delta (from here on, everything is delta higher) and diff[right + 1] -= delta (from here on, it isn't). The total change at i is then diff[0] + ... + diff[i], a prefix sum. So a range update became two point updates, and a point query became a prefix sum.

Step 2, a Fenwick tree for "point update, prefix sum". A Fenwick tree, or binary indexed tree (BIT), is an array tree[1..n], indexed from 1, where tree[i] holds the sum of the last lowbit(i) entries ending at i. lowbit(i) = i & -i is the value of i's lowest set bit (the lowest 1 bit): lowbit(6) = lowbit(110) = 2, so tree[6] covers positions 5 and 6; lowbit(8) = 8, so tree[8] covers 1 to 8.

add(i, delta): for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) tree[i] += delta. Adding the lowest set bit jumps to the next cell whose range also contains i: 3 -> 4 -> 8 -> 16.

prefix(i): for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) sum += tree[i]. Clearing the lowest set bit jumps to the cell just before this one's range: 7 -> 6 -> 4 -> 0, adding the ranges [7], [5..6] and [1..4].

Each loop runs at most once per bit of i, so both are O(log n). Two details. The tree is 1-indexed because lowbit(0) = 0 and i += 0 would loop forever, so shift array index i to tree index i + 1. And right + 1 can be past the end; skip that add (nothing after the array needs cancelling), or size the tree n + 1.

get(index) = nums[index] + prefix(index + 1). Keep the original nums; the tree only stores changes.

The harness builds new RangeAdder(nums), then runs "addRange" with [left, right, delta] and "get" with [index] in order, returning the get results. The visualization shows the tree array (cell 0 unused) during two range adds and a few gets.

visualizationSteps.message: nums = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. The array below is the Fenwick tree over the difference array, cells 1 to 9 (cell 0 is unused). tree[i] covers the lowbit(i) = i & -i positions ending at i.

addRange(2, 6, +5) becomes two point updates on the differences. First, at tree index 2 + 1 = 3: add(3, +5): touch 3 (11) -> 4 (100) -> 8 (1000), each time jumping i += i & -i to the next cell whose range covers 3.
Then the cancelling -5 at tree index 6 + 2 = 8: add(8, -5): touch 8 (1000), each time jumping i += i & -i to the next cell whose range covers 8.
get(4) = nums[4] + prefix(5) = tree[5]=0 + tree[4]=5 = 5, jumping i -= i & -i (clear the lowest set bit) until i is 0.
get(7) = nums[7] + prefix(8) = tree[8]=0 = 0, jumping i -= i & -i (clear the lowest set bit) until i is 0.
get(7) = 0 + 0 = 0: the +5 and -5 cancel after the range ends.
addRange(0, 3, +2): +2 at tree index 1, add(1, +2): touch 1 (1) -> 2 (10) -> 4 (100) -> 8 (1000), each time jumping i += i & -i to the next cell whose range covers 1.
and -2 at tree index 3 + 2 = 5: add(5, -2): touch 5 (101) -> 6 (110) -> 8 (1000), each time jumping i += i & -i to the next cell whose range covers 5.
get(2) = nums[2] + prefix(3) = tree[3]=5 + tree[2]=2 = 7, jumping i -= i & -i (clear the lowest set bit) until i is 0.
get(2) = 0 + 7 = 7: inside both ranges, 5 + 2. Every add and every get touched at most 4 cells, about log2(9).

recognitionSignals: Many "add x to every element in [l, r]" operations, mixed with reads of single elements.
A range update you could do with a difference array, except that queries come in between the updates.
Counting how many intervals cover a point, as the intervals arrive one by one.
gotchas: Fenwick trees are 1-indexed: i & -i is 0 for i = 0, so add(0, ...) never terminates. Use tree index = array index + 1.
The cancelling -delta goes at right + 1, not right; when right is the last index there is nothing to cancel.
get returns the original value plus the accumulated change, so keep a copy of nums.
If every update came before every query, a plain difference array and one prefix pass would be O(n + q) with no tree at all.
confusableWith: Segment Tree: Range Sum Query, Mutable (this track) is the opposite pairing: point update, range query. A Fenwick tree does that one directly with add and prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1).
Range add AND range sum together need either lazy propagation in a segment tree or two Fenwick trees (see Lazy Propagation in this track).

complexity.note: addRange is two Fenwick adds and get is one prefix sum, each a loop that runs once per bit of the index. The tree and the copy of nums are both O(n).
